29652:
Jesus of Nazareth was a Galilean Jew born near the end of Herod the Great's reign and executed by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea, around AD 30 or 33. After being baptized by John in the Jordan, he spent perhaps one to three years as a travelling teacher and healer, based in Capernaum and moving through Galilee, its neighbouring regions and finally Jerusalem. His central message was the arrival of the kingdom (reign) of God, taught through parables, memorable sayings and actions such as table fellowship with outsiders, healings and exorcisms. He gathered twelve disciples as a sign of Israel's renewal and drew both large crowds and sharp opposition.

The four Gospels present him as the promised Messiah and Son of God whose death was not an accident but the purpose of his mission: a ransom for many and the inauguration of a new covenant. All four end with the tomb found empty and with his followers' testimony that he was raised from the dead, the conviction that launched the Christian movement described in Acts and the letters of Paul.

Outside the New Testament, Jesus is mentioned by the Jewish historian Josephus and the Roman historian Tacitus, which is why nearly all historians accept that he existed and was crucified under Pilate. What he was, whether a prophet, the Messiah, God incarnate, or a teacher later idealized by his followers, is the question every tradition answers differently.
29653: The Gospels say Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of Mary while she was a virgin (Matt 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-38), in Bethlehem, and raised in Nazareth. He was baptized by John, proclaimed that the kingdom of God was at hand (Mark 1:14-15), taught with authority, healed the sick, cast out demons, ate with tax collectors and sinners, and called twelve disciples. He predicted his own suffering, death and resurrection (Mark 8:31). He was arrested in Jerusalem at Passover, tried before the high priest and before Pilate, crucified as 'King of the Jews', and buried. The Gospels report that on the third day the tomb was empty and that he appeared alive to many (Matt 28; Luke 24; John 20-21; 1 Cor 15:3-8). John's Gospel calls him the eternal Word who became flesh (John 1:1-14); Paul says he was in the form of God and emptied himself (Phil 2:5-11).
29655: Jesus is the eternal Son of God, one divine person in two natures, fully God and fully human, as defined at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451). His death and resurrection reconcile humanity to God; Orthodox theology especially stresses incarnation and resurrection as the healing and deification (theosis) of human nature, while Catholic theology also stresses the sacrificial character of the cross made present in the Eucharist.
29657: Affirms the same Nicene and Chalcedonian Christology. Places strong emphasis on Christ's substitutionary death as the ground of justification by grace through faith, and on his threefold office as prophet, priest and king. Scripture alone is the authority for knowing him.

The Christian doctrines of incarnation and Trinity are seen as incompatible with the oneness of God (Deut 6:4).

Almost all accept his baptism by John and his crucifixion under Pilate as secure historical facts.

29670: Jesus lived in a Judea divided after Herod the Great's death: Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, while Judea itself was under a Roman prefect from AD 6, with the temple run by a high-priestly aristocracy (Annas, Caiaphas). Jewish groups included Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and later Zealot-leaning revolutionaries; hopes for a messianic deliverer took many forms. Galilee was largely Jewish and agrarian, with fishing on the lake and new Hellenistic cities like Sepphoris and Tiberias. Jesus taught mostly in Aramaic and knew the Hebrew Scriptures; Greek was the language of trade and of the Gospels. Josephus (Antiquities 18.63-64, partly interpolated by later Christian scribes, and 20.200) and Tacitus (Annals 15.44) are the earliest non-Christian witnesses.
29671: Christianity, now the largest religion in the world, takes its name from Jesus as the Christ. His teaching (the Sermon on the Mount, the Lord's Prayer, the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son) shaped Western ethics, law and art. The calendar division BC/AD is reckoned from an estimate of his birth made by Dionysius Exiguus in the 6th century, which turned out to be several years too late. Jesus is also honoured in Islam as the prophet Isa, born of the virgin Mary.

Mary was a young Jewish woman of Nazareth, betrothed to the craftsman Joseph, when, according to Luke and Matthew, she conceived Jesus by the Holy Spirit without a human father. Luke tells the story largely from her side: the angel's announcement, her consent, her song of praise (the Magnificat), the birth in Bethlehem and her quiet pondering of what she saw.

During Jesus' ministry she appears only occasionally: prompting his first sign at Cana, seeking him with his brothers, and standing at the cross, where John's Gospel says Jesus entrusted her to the beloved disciple. Acts places her among the praying believers in Jerusalem before Pentecost, and after that Scripture is silent.

Few figures have been so variously understood. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians she is the Theotokos, the ever-virgin Mother of God and the model disciple, honoured in liturgy and prayer; for most Protestants she is a supreme example of faith but not an object of devotion; for Muslims she is Maryam, the most honoured woman in the Quran.
29728: Mary is called a virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David (Luke 1:27; Matt 1:18). She conceives by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35; Matt 1:20) and is called 'favoured' and 'blessed among women' (Luke 1:28; Luke 1:42). Elizabeth is her relative (Luke 1:36). She gives birth in Bethlehem, is warned by Simeon of a sword piercing her soul (Luke 2:35), and twice is said to treasure things in her heart (Luke 2:19; Luke 2:51). Jesus is called 'the son of Mary' and is said to have brothers named James, Joses, Judas and Simon, and sisters (Mark 6:3). She is at the cross (John 19:25) and with the disciples in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14). The New Testament records nothing of her parents, later life or death.
29729: Mary is Mother of God (Council of Ephesus, 431), perpetually virgin, preserved from original sin from conception (Immaculate Conception, defined 1854) and assumed body and soul into heaven (Assumption, defined 1950). She is honoured (hyperdulia, not worship) as intercessor and Mother of the Church. Jesus' 'brothers' are read as cousins or relatives.
29730: Venerates Mary as Theotokos and Ever-Virgin, 'more honourable than the cherubim', and celebrates her Dormition (falling asleep) and bodily translation to heaven, without defining it as dogma in the Catholic manner. Generally does not adopt the Immaculate Conception doctrine. The 'brothers' are often read as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage.

Many today read Mark 6:3 and Matt 1:25 as indicating that Mary and Joseph had other children, though Luther, Zwingli and some early Reformers affirmed her perpetual virginity.
